metadata.title: Replication Package for "Hidden Dependencies in LLM-Enabled Code Generation: An Empirical Study of Regressions and Escaped Failures"
metadata.description:
Replication package accompanying the ESEM 2026 paper "Hidden Dependencies in LLM-Enabled Code Generation: An Empirical Study of Regressions and Escaped Failures" (Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics, LIPIcs, Vol. 394).

The archive contains the experiment configurations; frozen task-selection records and rendered experimental conditions; raw model generations; evaluation records for the three oracle layers (O1, O2, and O3); archived pre-correction evaluator snapshots retained for sensitivity analyses; analysis and integrity-checking scripts; result tables; the figures used in the paper; run-family provenance records; and the post-acceptance audit records PA-00-PA-06 together with their recorded outputs and hashes.

Start with README.md. REPRODUCE_CORE_RESULTS.md gives the shortest path to the main quantitative results, REPRODUCE.md describes the full reproduction workflow, and CLAIMS_TO_ARTIFACTS.md maps each quantitative claim in the paper to the corresponding scripts, inputs, and outputs.

Source code is released under the MIT License. Derived data are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0) unless a more restrictive upstream license applies. Materials derived from HumanEval, MBPP, CodeRAG-Bench, and EvalPlus remain subject to their respective upstream licenses. Model weights are not redistributed; public model identifiers and the available provenance records are included in the archive.

metadata.title: Replication Package for the ISSRE 2026 Paper "From Discussion to Execution: Replicating Buggy and Correct Data Science Code"
metadata.description:
This replication package accompanies the ISSRE 2026 paper “From Discussion to Execution: Replicating Buggy and Correct Data Science Code.”

The artifact contains the datasets, source code, prompts, isolated execution environment, evaluation scripts, and supporting results used to evaluate Reprodgen, an LLM-based framework for reconstructing executable buggy and patched data science programs from informal developer discussions such as Stack Overflow posts and GitHub Issues. The package includes ReprodgenBench-B, the human-validated benchmark artifacts, the ReprodgenBench-GI GitHub-Issue dataset, the Generator–Reviewer pipeline, Docker-based Python execution support, and scripts for computing Execution Rate (ER), Success Rate (SR), CodeBERTScore, and Levenshtein Distance. It also contains the figures, precomputed experimental results, and supplementary state-of-the-art comparison material associated with the paper. The included README provides environment setup instructions, a deterministic smoke test, a bounded reproduction example, and commands for regenerating and evaluating experimental outputs. The artifact is intended to support independent inspection, execution, and reproduction of the empirical results reported in the paper.

metadata.title: Replication package for "Do Age Restrictions Target the Right Cohort? Verification Behaviour and Digital Exposure Across the EU-27"
metadata.description:
Replication package for the article "Do Age Restrictions Target the Right Cohort? Verification Behaviour and Digital Exposure Across the EU-27". Contains a single Python script reproducing every result reported in the article and its Supporting Information, together with the console output of that script and the exact library versions used.

The analysis uses Flash Eurobarometer 3592 (GESIS study ZA9078, dataset version 1-0-0), a survey of 26,114 citizens across the 27 European Union member states conducted in June 2025. The survey data are not included in this package: they are distributed by the GESIS Data Archive under its own terms of use and must be obtained from there. The README documents how to obtain the file and describes three coding decisions in the source data that materially affect substantive conclusions.

metadata.title: Replication package for the study "The Usage of the C Preprocessor in the Linux Kernel"
metadata.description:
The Usage of the C Preprocessor in Linux Kernel: Replication package

This replication package contains code and data associated with the study “You Are not Expected to Understand this: The Usage of the C Preprocessor in the Linux Kernel”.

The provided files are organized as follows.

  • README.md: A file containing the text you are reading.
  • Makefile: Rules for running the analysis SQL queries and Python scripts.
  • footnotes.pdf: The publication annotated with footnotes for all source code references, scripts, and obtained results.
  • obj-macro-to-enum.patch: A patch against Linux kernel v7.1 converting object-like macros into enum members.
  • requirements.txt: Used Python packages.
  • cache-run.py: Program to run the above commands and cache their results. This allows the analysis to be performed on one host, pushed to a Git repository, and pulled from another.
  • plots: Python, shell scripts, and data for creating the publication’s figures.
  • scripts: Data analytics SQL and Python scripts for creating individual numbers and tables included in the publication. To understand what each script does look in the publication for the corresponding footnote.
  • results: Output of the above scripts.
  • data: Additional data files required for the above scripts.
  • refactor-obj: Proof of concept for automated refactoring of object-like macros into C enumerations.
  • rust: Rust programs demonstrating features that supplant tricky functionality found in C function-like macros.
  • src: Shell scripts and SLURM files for compiling and analyzing the Linux kernel. (See earlier versions of this package for a starting point on performing the analysis on a supercomputer.)
  • linux-7.1/linux-*.cs: CScout configuration files used for analyzing each configuration of the Linux kernel. These are compiler and host specific, and are therefore provided for reference only. The CScout runs can be replicated through the procedures in the following section.

metadata.title: Software Package for "WIP: Block-Based Programming Increases Student's Success Rate in Solving Assembly Programming Tasks"
metadata.description:
Blocksembler Deployment

This repository provides the required Docker Compose files and configuration files to run a complete Blocksembler deployment. It includes all necessary services, including the frontend, API backend, database, message queue, and supporting components, enabling a reproducible setup of the Blocksembler environment.

Prerequisites

To run Blocksembler, make sure that both docker and docker compose are installed on your machine.

We recommend following the official installation instructions:

https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/

🚀 Start Services

docker compose -f compose.yml -f compose.leonding.yml up -d

📊 Import Competition Data

To initialize the database to the state used during the competition, first open an interactive shell in the database container:

docker exec -it blocksembler-db /bin/bash

The script that imports all competition data is already mounted into the database container (db_scripts/create.sql). Run the script using the following command:

psql -U postgres -d blocksembler -f ./db_scripts/create.sql

💻 Start Exploring Blocksembler

To start exploring Blocksembler, open your favorite browser and visit http://localhost.

The create.sql script was modified that it configured four tan codes that can be used to explore the system:

TAN Code Description
bbp-warmup Warmup exercises in the block-based condition
tbp-warmup Warmup exercises in the text-based condition
bbp-comp Main competition in the block-based condition
tbp-comp Main competition in the text-based condition

Remark: This version of the blocksembler-deployment repository represents the version that was used for the Blocksembler Coding Competition held on 10 February 2026 at HTL Leonding, Austria. However, the configuration file (leonding.env) initially pointed to the wrong backend. This issue was fixed on-site, and the correction was later added to the repository when preparing the replication package for publication alongside the paper reporting the results of this coding competition.

metadata.title: Replication package for "An empirical study of post-quantum signature transport cost under IP fragmentation in reliable DDS"
metadata.description:
Replication package for the paper "An empirical study of post-quantum signature transport cost under IP fragmentation in reliable DDS".

The archive contains everything needed to re-derive every number in every table of the paper from the raw measurements, without access to the testbed: the measurement probes for both DDS implementations, every analysis and verification script, the raw CSV output of all 1510 runs, the packet captures the mechanism section rests on, the XML profiles each arm was configured with, and the complete record of the twenty-five instrumentation and analysis defects found during the study, each paired with the symptom that exposed it.

Measurements were taken on Raspberry Pi 4B nodes running Eclipse Cyclone DDS and eProsima Fast DDS 3.1.2 with liboqs, under emulated independent and bursty loss.

Re-deriving the published numbers requires no hardware: verify_tables.py recomputes every table from the CSVs and quantisation_test.py --check-paper recomputes the two-implementation analysis and fails if any published value differs.

 

v1.2.0 adds code/make_transfer_table.py, which generates the cross-implementation summary table of the manuscript from the raw CSVs. No other file changed and the measurement data are unchanged.

metadata.title: Replication package for the Technical Report: Do Stack Overflow Answer Edits Occur Beyond Java? A Replication on Python and JavaScript
metadata.description:
Replication Package — Do Stack Overflow Answer Edits Occur Beyond Java? A Replication on Python and JavaScript

Chaiyong Ragkhitwetsagul, In-on Wiratsin, Matheus Paixao, Denis De Sousa, Pongpop Lapvikai, Peter Haddawy

Faculty of Information and Communication Technology, Mahidol University, Thailand · State University of Ceara (UECE), Brazil

This package contains the data, code, intermediate results, and report source for replicating the Java study by Wiratsin et al. (arXiv:2511.05813) in Python and JavaScript.

The study asks two questions:

  • RQ1 — How often are accepted Stack Overflow answers edited, and how large are the edits to their code snippets?
  • RQ2 — Do the resulting code recommendations concentrate in popular GitHub projects?

Headline results, over 840,132 accepted Python answers and 1,144,185 accepted JavaScript answers from the SOTorrent 2020-12-31 release: 41.25% and 39.10% respectively have been edited at least once, against 16.11% for Java, while the mean number of revisions per edited answer is nearly identical across the three languages (2.78, 2.68, 2.82). Searching 100 GitHub projects per language, matched answer edits rise monotonically from low- to medium- to high-popularity projects — 80 / 156 / 977 for Python and 32 / 71 / 353 for JavaScript — significantly so for Python, not for JavaScript.

The full report is replication_study.pdf.

What is in the package

replication_study.pdf         The technical report (built PDF)
README.md                     This file
CITATION.cff                  Citation metadata
LICENSE                       MIT, applies to the code
requirements.txt              Python dependencies
MANIFEST.sha256               SHA-256 of every file in the package

analysis/                     Analysis code and data
  extract_answer_list.py        Stage 1: select accepted, revised answers from SOTorrent
  python_revision_extraction.ipynb    Stage 2: extract code-block revisions to files
  javascript_revision_extraction.ipynb
  python_rq1_stats.ipynb        Stage 3: RQ1 statistics and Levenshtein distances
  javascript_rq1_stats.ipynb
  python_rq1_stats.py           Command-line equivalent of the Python RQ1 notebook
  levenshtein_stats.py          Stage 4: edit-size distribution, no database needed
  aggregate_so_gh_clones.py     Stage 5: RQ2 aggregation and statistical tests
  levenshtein_distances_python.csv       637,923 original/latest code-block pairs
  levenshtein_distances_javascript.csv   793,362 pairs
  python_post_revisions_histogram.pdf    Revision-count histograms (report Figs. 1-2)
  javascript_post_revisions_histogram.pdf
  so-gh_clones/                 RQ2 clone-search output
    {python,javascript}_repos_stars*.txt      the 100 searched projects per language,
                                              split into the three popularity groups
    search_results_python_new/    one CSV of matched clone pairs per Python project
    search_results_js/            one CSV per JavaScript project

files/                        Answer id lists produced by stage 1
  acceptedWithVersionAnswer_python.txt        305,768 ids (see the caveat below)
  acceptedWithVersionAnswer_javascript.txt    447,379 ids, unrestricted

results/                      Derived results, regenerated when this package was built
  levenshtein_stats.{json,txt}  Stage 4 output
  rq2_summary.{json,txt}        Stage 5 output

technical-report/             Report source, buildable with `make`
  report.tex, references.bib, Makefile
  make_figures.py               Stage 6: regenerates the figures
  figures/                      Figures used by the report
  rq2_summary.json              Stage 5 output, consumed by make_figures.py
  notes-paper.md                Notes on the Java manuscript being replicated
  notes-results-python.md       RQ1 results, Python
  notes-results-javascript.md   RQ1 results, JavaScript
  notes-rq2-clones.md           RQ2 clone-search results

The four notes-*.md files are the authority for every number in the report: they were written directly from tool output. Where the report and a notes file disagree, trust the notes file.

Reproducing the results

The directory layout matters — the scripts resolve their inputs relative to their own location, so run them from within the unpacked package without moving files.

Stages 1 to 3 need a local SOTorrent database. Stages 4 to 7 run from the CSVs shipped here, so every number and figure in the report can be reproduced without MySQL.

Prerequisites

For stages 4 to 7 only:

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt

For stages 1 to 3 additionally: MySQL with the SOTorrent 2020-12-31 release loaded into a schema named sotorrent, reachable at 127.0.0.1 as user root with an empty password. Change the connection settings in the configuration cell of each notebook if yours differ. SOTorrent is available at https://empirical-software.engineering/projects/sotorrent/.

For stage 7: LaTeX with the IEEEtran class. TeX Live 2025 has it.

1. Select the accepted, revised answers (database, ~10 min per language)

.venv/bin/python3 analysis/extract_answer_list.py --tag python \
    --output files/acceptedWithVersionAnswer_python.txt
.venv/bin/python3 analysis/extract_answer_list.py --tag javascript \
    --output files/acceptedWithVersionAnswer_javascript.txt

An answer is selected when it is accepted, its parent question carries the tag, and it has at least one PostVersion row with a non-null PredPostHistoryId — that is, it was edited at least once. This is the predicate the Java study used.

Caveat. Do not pass --require-code-block. The Python list shipped here was built with that flag, which is why it holds 305,768 ids while the unrestricted query returns 346,535. The report quotes 41.25% (unrestricted) as the RQ1 headline for Python, because that is the quantity the Java study reports, and 36.40% as the code-bearing subset. The JavaScript list is unrestricted and needs no such caveat. See technical-report/notes-results-python.md section 5.

2. Extract the code block revisions (database, ~8-11 min per language)

Open analysis/python_revision_extraction.ipynb and analysis/javascript_revision_extraction.ipynb, set RUN_FULL_EXTRACTION = True, and run all cells. Each writes one directory per answer to ../python_files/ and ../javascript_files/, one level above the package root, containing one file per code block revision plus _original and _recent files per (PostId, LocalId) pair.

Extraction is resumable: an answer whose output directory already exists is skipped. Expect roughly 2.9 million files for Python and 3.6 million for JavaScript. These extracted files are not shipped here — they are ~10 GB per language and are fully derivable from SOTorrent.

3. RQ1 statistics and edit distances (database, ~20 min per language)

Open analysis/python_rq1_stats.ipynb and analysis/javascript_rq1_stats.ipynb and run all cells. Set RUN_DISTANCE_COMPUTATION = True in the Levenshtein cell to rebuild the distance CSVs; leave it False to reuse the ones shipped here, which is much faster.

These notebooks produce the accepted-answer totals, code snippet counts, revision counts and headline Levenshtein figures, and they write analysis/levenshtein_distances_{python,javascript}.csv and the revision histograms.

The notebooks select the filtered answer set from the database rather than reading the id file, and cross-check the id file against the query result. Running the Python notebook against the shipped list will therefore report 346,535 answers and warn that the file holds 305,768. That warning is expected and is the discrepancy described in stage 1.

analysis/python_rq1_stats.py is a command-line equivalent of the Python notebook:

.venv/bin/python3 analysis/python_rq1_stats.py --tag python

4. Edit-size distribution (no database, ~1 min)

.venv/bin/python3 analysis/levenshtein_stats.py --json results/levenshtein_stats.json

Derives the parts of the distribution the notebooks do not: the proportion of code blocks byte-identical between their original and latest revisions, the distribution restricted to blocks that did change, selected quantiles, and the per-answer aggregates. Uses only the standard library.

5. RQ2, the clone search results (no database, ~1 min)

The clone search itself was run separately with Siamese+/Matcha; its output is included under analysis/so-gh_clones/ as one CSV per project plus the three project lists per language. Re-running the search requires Matcha (https://github.com/cragkhit/Matcha) and local clones of the 200 projects; the tuned configuration is the one from the Java study, given in Section II-D of the report.

To aggregate the included results:

.venv/bin/python3 analysis/aggregate_so_gh_clones.py --json results/rq2_summary.json

This maps each project to its popularity group, counts candidate pairs, matched blocks, and matched answer edits per group, computes per-project maxima and averages, and runs the Shapiro-Wilk and Kruskal-Wallis tests. scipy is needed for the tests; without it, the counts are still produced, and the tests are skipped.

6. Figures (no database, ~1 min)

.venv/bin/python3 technical-report/make_figures.py

Writes the Levenshtein boxplots and the RQ2 bar chart into technical-report/figures/, invoking the stage 5 aggregation for the latter. The two revision histograms are copied from analysis/ rather than regenerated, because the per-answer revision counts exist only in the database.

7. Build the report

cd technical-report && make

Runs pdflatex, bibtex, then pdflatex twice more. make figures reruns stage 6 and make clean removes the build artefacts. A clean build produces a 12-page PDF with no undefined references and no bibtex warnings.

Where each number in the report comes from

Report location Numbers Produced by
Table III, rows 1 to 9 Accepted answers, snippets, revision counts, maxima Stage 3 notebooks
Table III, Levenshtein rows Mean, median, maximum, standard deviation Stage 3 notebooks
Table III, unchanged code blocks 68.68%, 67.70% Stage 4
Section III-A, III-B, quantiles and changed-only figures p75, p90, p95, p99, changed-only mean and median Stage 4
Section III-A, III-B, per-answer aggregates Answers with pairs, blocks per answer, answers with a changed block Stage 4
Tables I and II All RQ2 counts, maxima and averages Stage 5
Section III-A, III-B, Kruskal-Wallis and Shapiro-Wilk H, p, W Stage 5
Figures 1 and 2 Revision histograms Stage 3, copied by stage 6
Figures 3 and 4 Boxplots, RQ2 bar chart Stage 6
All Java figures Everything in the Java column The original manuscript, not recomputed

Data formats

analysis/levenshtein_distances_{lang}.csv — one row per code block, header First File,Second File,Levenshtein Distance. The two path columns name the original and latest revision of the same (PostId, LocalId) code block, as written by stage 2; the answer id is the parent directory name and the LocalId is the middle field of the filename. The third column is the character-level Levenshtein distance, 0 when the block was never textually changed.

analysis/so-gh_clones/search_results_*/{repo}_{timestamp}.csv — one file per searched GitHub project, holding the candidate clone pairs the search returned between that project and the indexed Stack Overflow code-block revisions.

files/acceptedWithVersionAnswer_{lang}.txt — one Stack Overflow answer id per line, ascending.

Reproducibility caveats

These are stated in the report's threats to validity and repeated here because they affect what a re-run will show.

  • The clone-search configuration is the one tuned for Java in the original study, against a 2013 Java ground truth. No language-specific retuning was done, so match counts are comparable across the three languages but are not optimal for Python or JavaScript.
  • The popularity thresholds are inherited from the Java project population rather than recomputed as quartiles of the Python or JavaScript populations.
  • 100 projects per language were searched, against the Java study's 10,673. Absolute counts are therefore not comparable with the published Java figures; only the within-study distribution across groups is.
  • No manual classification was performed. The RQ2 figures are candidate matches, so they correspond to the Java study's 793 candidate pairs, not to its 391 manually validated applicable recommendations.
  • The SOTorrent release is 2020-12-31, so the data predate the widespread adoption of generative AI coding assistants.
  • The Python answer id list was built with --require-code-block, as described in stage 1.

Licence

Code in this package is released under the MIT license (LICENSE).

The derived data files are released under CC BY-SA 4.0, following the license of the Stack Overflow content they are derived from via SOTorrent. Stack Overflow content is contributed by its users under CC BY-SA; SOTorrent itself is distributed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

Citing

See CITATION.cff. The study being replicated is:

In-on Wiratsin, Chaiyong Ragkhitwetsagul, Matheus Paixao, Denis De Sousa, Pongpop Lapvikai, and Peter Haddawy. An Empirical Study of Java Code Improvements Based on Stack Overflow Answer Edits. arXiv:2511.05813, 2025.

The underlying dataset is:

Sebastian Baltes, Lorik Dumani, Christoph Treude, and Stephan Diehl. SOTorrent: Reconstructing and Analyzing the Evolution of Stack Overflow Posts. MSR 2018, 319-330. doi:10.1145/3196398.3196430

metadata.title: Replication package for "Conformal Calibration of Uncertainty Sets for Robust Portfolio Choice: A Closed-Form Second-Order Cone Program under Markov-Switching GARCH"
metadata.description:
Code and derived results reproducing every table, figure and quoted number in the manuscript "Conformal Calibration of Uncertainty Sets for Robust Portfolio Choice: A Closed-Form Second-Order Cone Program under Markov-Switching GARCH".

The pipeline calibrates the uncertainty set of a robust portfolio rule from data rather than postulating it. A two-regime Markov-switching GARCH model supplies regime-conditional moments; split conformal prediction converts their estimation errors into uncertainty sets with a finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantee; the resulting worst-case Merton allocation is solved in closed form as a second-order cone program, with a tri-objective NSGA-II layer tracing the surrounding frontier. The empirical study covers eight US-listed agricultural futures over 2003-2025 (5,563 daily observations, 268 monthly rebalancing dates) with a cross-domain validation on four energy futures.

Contents: the full R pipeline (stages 01-19, including solver utilities and test gates); fitted MSGARCH objects, regime labels, parameter estimates, conformal radii, NSGA-II Pareto fronts and backtest weights; every CSV behind a table in the manuscript; the published figures; and NUMBERS.md, which maps each headline figure to the file it is computed from.

Raw price series are not redistributed. Daily settlements come from Yahoo Finance, whose terms do not permit redistribution, and daily log-returns are an invertible transform of them. The README documents the exact tickers, sample window, transformation and seed needed to reconstruct them, and the deposited model artifacts allow the analysis to be re-run from the backtest stage onward without downloading anything.

Idle cash is credited at the realized Federal Funds effective rate, the same time-varying series subtracted to form excess returns, so a cash position is Sharpe-neutral by construction. The unit and length guards in the configuration and backtest stages exist to keep that invariant and fail loudly rather than silently recycling a mismatched rate vector.

metadata.title: Who Fails the Filter? Size, Verification and the Incidence of Minimum Legal Capital: Replication package
metadata.description:
Processing code, a codebook and a SHA-256 manifest of the source archives for a study of the incidence of Brazil's minimum capital requirement for the single-owner limited-liability company (EIRELI), computed on the Receita Federal do Brasil's open CNPJ register.

Contents: the analysis code, 54 scripts run in batch and 2 run by hand; CODEBOOK.md, documenting every variable read and constructed, the coded values the analysis depends on, and six questions this register cannot answer; a SHA-256 manifest of all 308 source archives, of which the 58 archives of the July 2026 and May 2023 extractions carry the reported results; the derived tables the figures are drawn from; and the captured output of all 56 scripts, so that each reported number can be checked without downloading the 10 GB of source data.

The source data are not redistributed here. They are the Receita Federal's public CNPJ extractions, retained on the official share for a rolling thirty-nine months. The manifest hashes the archives as published, so it identifies a byte-identical copy; it will not match a mirror that has re-compressed the same contents.

Licensing is split. The code in code/ is under the MIT licence. The manifest, derived tables, logs, figures and documentation are under CC BY 4.0. See LICENSE and LICENSE-DATA.txt.

A full rebuild took 2h02m on an Apple M2 Max under Python 3.13.1. README.md gives the environment of record; CHECKLIST.md records known limitations, including one script whose live SIDRA API call no longer succeeds and whose outputs therefore ship with the package.

metadata.title: BusRecall: replication package for "What adaptation costs: source-vehicle forgetting in cross-vehicle CAN intrusion detection"
metadata.description: Code and result files for the paper "What adaptation costs: source-vehicle forgetting in cross-vehicle CAN intrusion detection". The package reproduces every table and figure in the paper: the cross-vehicle collapse and its three controls, the continual-learning comparison over all 24 task orders on two independent corpora (can-train-and-test and the ORNL ROAD dataset), the diagnostic measurement of the distillation teacher on the target vehicle, and the memory-budget curve. The two datasets are public and are not redistributed here; the README gives their DOIs and the pipeline that builds the caches.

metadata.title: MDEO-Cloud: A Modular Cloud-Based Platform for Model-Driven Optimization - Replication Package
metadata.description:
This replication package contains the software and data used in the evluation of the paper "MDEO-Cloud: A Modular Cloud-Based Platform for Model-Driven Optimization" by Niklas Krieger, Sandro Speth, Steffen Becker, and Steffen Zschaler

Content

  • three case studies used during the user study and experiments
  • software to run scalability and quality comparisons
  • user study instructions, task description, survey, and results
  • docker compose file to run the platform
